source.title: Reproducing and Evaluating the Generalizability of Subliminal Learning in Open-Weight Models
source.citation: Daan van der Weijden et al., 2026
source.authors: Daan van der Weijden; Nathan Brack; Selene Baez Santamaria

page_placements.theme: Behaviour shifts from fine-tuning itself (control baselines)
Content-level checks fail to detect or remove the signal

record.tranche_reason: Reproduces the original teacher-data generation, filtering, same-base student fine-tuning, and neutral-prompt trait evaluation on open-weight models; it also extends the setup.
record.gate_note: The paper reports behavioral results for filtered teacher outputs and a probe of teacher datasets. It also reports completion-health categories, but those do not measure whether students acquire the target preference, so they are not recorded as preference-transmission rows. Figure 2 and Figure 3 values are not present as readable numbers in the supplied text; where only their plotted results are available, values are recorded as figure only.
record.test_reason: Reproduces the original animal-numbers pipeline, using the original code base with same-base students, on Qwen2.5-7B and Gemma3-4B. It extends this to actors, politicians, chess, Ministral8B and answer-space size, and reports target-entity naming rates and log-odds ratios against regular-FT students. These bear directly on version A.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that subliminal learning reproduces and is real, but its magnitude depends on trait, task and model. It survives a non-numerical chess task, strengthens as the answer space shrinks, and is nearly absent in Ministral. They frame this as qualifying rather than overturning the original claims.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the original distillation pipeline with minimal adaptation, but substitutes accessible open-weight models for the unavailable GPT-4.x fine-tuning setup and adds actor/politician traits, chess generation, Ministral8B, and answer-space ablations.
record.method_sensitivity: Transmission varies by trait, task, and model; numbers generally produce stronger effects than chess, and smaller number answer spaces generally produce stronger effects, with panda as an exception.

fits_no_version.finding: A logistic-regression probe separates panda-teacher number sequences from control sequences at AUC 0.53, near chance. The number-frequency peaks are shared by trait and control data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Trait-bearing teacher data is not distinguishable from control data by simple distributional probes.

fits_no_version.finding: Under the animal trait-FT condition, Qwen's valid-answer rate falls from about 99% to about 50%, with the rest classed as other or identity leak. Under politician trait-FT, Qwen's refusals drop from about 20-25%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Subliminal fine-tuning changes answer format and refusal behaviour beyond the target preference.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 9th BlackboxNLP Workshop: Analyzing and Interpreting Neural Networks for NLP
record.problems: The study uses only three open-weight model families, and results are not directly comparable model-for-model with the original GPT-4.x experiments. Entity selection for the new categories involves researcher heuristics. Chess filtering does not verify board-state legality. The teacher-generated dataset is fixed rather than resampled across fine-tuning seeds. Confidence intervals are across five fine-tuning seeds, and the authors do not correct for multiple comparisons across entities. Several plotted values are not provided numerically in the text supplied.

untested.parts: All students share the teacher's reference model; no cross-base condition.
No misalignment or harmful traits tested.
No test of token entanglement, divergence tokens, steering-vector directions or a gradient argument; the probe only checks dataset separability.
Only LoRA rank 8; no full fine-tuning and no rank sweep. Evaluation uses the original's standard neutral preference prompts, not a robustness manipulation.

missing.what: Per-entity log-odds ratios and confidence intervals for all model × task × category cells. Needed to check the per-row states, which currently rest on aggregate text statements.
Per-target log-odds values at 1-, 2- and 3-digit answer spaces
Completion-health proportions: Qwen animal trait-FT valid answers about 50% vs about 99%; Qwen politician refusals 20-25% at base and control, dropping under trait-FT
missing.versions: none (side effect; affects interpretation of A rates)

record.verdict_notes: The reader's E 'supports' label is dropped. Evaluating on neutral preference prompts is the original protocol, not a robustness test, and only LoRA rank 8 is used. Version codes V1, V4 and V5 are remapped to letters. Most per-cell states are figure-only and rest on the authors' aggregate statements. The study does not correct for multiple comparisons, and the teacher dataset is fixed across seeds, so the CIs reflect only fine-tuning variance.

versions.untested_parts: Tests animal, actor, and politician preferences on numbers and chess, using three open-weight model families. Does not test every trait or modality in the original work.
Teacher and student share the same reference model in all experiments; no different-base student condition is tested.
No misalignment or other harmful/alignment-relevant trait is tested.

Tests whether teacher number sequences are distinguishable with a logistic-regression probe and whether number-frequency peaks are shared by trait and control data. Does not test token entanglement, divergence tokens, steering-vector-like directions, or a gradient mechanism.
Evaluates with neutral prompt variants not mentioning the trait. Tests only LoRA rank 8; does not compare full fine-tuning with LoRA or sweep LoRA ranks.
No prompt-only insertion of linked tokens without fine-tuning.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned a same-reference-model student on filtered animal-specific number sequences from a persona-primed teacher; compared with regular-FT and base.

conditions.value: 50 neutral prompt variants; 5,000 completions per condition

rows.measure: Rate of naming the target animal as favorite
rows.baseline: regular-FT and base conditions shown in Figure 1; numeric values not stated
rows.value: Figure 1 reports that animal-number fine-tuning raises the target-animal naming rate; numeric value not stated
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals across seeds shown in Figure 1; interval values not stated
rows.note: The authors say the reproduction confirms the subliminal-transmission effect, with some quantitative differences from the original.
rows.check: Version code V1/V5 should be A only. Neutral preference prompts are the original's standard evaluation, not a robustness test of E. Figure 1 says each target rate rises, but §4.2.1 reports negative log-odds for Qwen elephant, dog and tiger. The study does not reconcile the two.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B
rows.operation_detail: Compared one-, two-, and three-digit number-sequence answer spaces in the animal preference setup.
rows.measure: Log-odds ratio of target entity naming, trait-FT versus regular-FT
rows.value: Figure 3 values not stated in text; effect rises as digit space shrinks, except panda
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals plotted; numeric values not stated
rows.note: The reported trend is stronger transmission with smaller answer spaces, with panda as the stated exception.
rows.check: Relink V1 to A. This is a modulator result: LOR rises as the digit space shrinks, except panda. Values are figure-only, and per-target signs at each length are not stated.

source_check.correct: observed: authors say LOR 'rises consistently as the digit space shrinks', transmission 'growing stronger rather than weaker', and only panda breaks the trend. Per-target values are figure-only.
source_check.problem: Nothing in the text says the effect is incomplete or weaker. Transmission strengthens at smaller answer spaces, so partial is not supported.

rows.subject: Logistic-regression probe
rows.operation_detail: Trained a probe to distinguish trait-generated number sequences from control sequences.
rows.measure: AUC for distinguishing trait from control sequences
rows.uncertainty: not stated
rows.note: The authors describe the distributions as not meaningfully separable and say their shared non-uniformity is inherent to the task, not preference-specific.
rows.check: The probe measures whether teacher data is distinguishable from control data, not student trait acquisition. It does not test token entanglement, divergence tokens, a steering direction or a gradient argument, so it is not a test of D. It is recorded under fits_no_version.

source_check.problem: The probe's panda/N=30,000 setting comes from the adjacent Fig. 4 caption; it is not stated for the probe itself. versions=none is defensible.

tranche.reason: It reruns the original's Qwen2.5-7B animal-numbers experiment (Extended Data Fig. 5c) with the original code base, the same-base students, the same measure and a regular-FT control. The extensions are additions on top of that.

source_check.notes: The only numbers in the text are Trump 0.06%->78% (LOR 8.6) and probe AUC 0.53; everything else is figure-only. The Fig. 1 caption (each target animal rises) conflicts with Fig. 2's negative LORs for elephant, dog and tiger on Qwen numbers, and the text does not resolve this. Fig. 1 reproduces Qwen only, not Gemma. The completion-health results (Qwen animal trait-FT valid answers about 99%->50%; Llama3.1-8B judge) have no row.

statements.correction: arXiv:2609.12586, Qwen2.5-7B, Trump: regular-FT about 0.06%, trait-FT about 78%, LOR about 8.6 (§4.2.1). Task (numbers or chess) not stated. Code and 95% t-intervals over 5 seeds hold for the study overall.
statements.problem: Numbers and model are right, but the text does not name the task for the Trump example. 'number sequences' is an inference. No CI is given for this example.

statements.correction: arXiv:2609.12586: chess gives an effect 'similar to, though generally weaker than' numbers (§5). The numbers-chess gap is far larger for Qwen than for Gemma (§4.2.1). Values are figure-only. This is limits_scope, not challenges.
statements.problem: The part citing this study is cut off. It cites R3 (Qwen animal chess) under a challenges label, but chess transmission is present, only weaker than numbers. The authors say the effect survives a non-numerical task. Other chess rows (R5, R7, R9, R11, R13) are not cited.
Caveat: the authors say per-entity CIs are not multiplicity-corrected and are not independent significance tests (A.5). The Fig. 1 caption also says the fine-tune raises each target's rate.
The panda-teacher pairing is implied by the Fig. 4 context; it is not stated for the probe itself.
